transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming today. To start off, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me?

Hi, doctor. Thank you so much for taking the time to see me. Um, well, I guess I'm here because... well, I've just been feeling a bit, I don't know, overly energetic lately? I mean, I teach special education, so staying busy is just part of the job, and I've always prided myself on being a hard worker. 

But lately, it's... well, it feels almost like I'm constantly running on a motor, if that makes sense. Like I’ll finish one task at school, or even just chores around the house, and I immediately jump right into the next thing. I just can't seem to shut myself off at the end of the day. I mean, it's great for getting things done, obviously, but... I don't know, is that the sort of thing people usually come in here for? I hope I'm explaining it okay.
Have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual to feel rested during this time?

Oh, um, no, I wouldn't say that. I definitely still need a good night's rest. If I don't get my usual, you know, seven or eight hours, I feel pretty wiped out the next day just like anyone else would. 

It's really just that getting myself to actually stop and get into bed is the tricky part. But I certainly don't feel rested on just a few hours of sleep, if that's what you mean. I try to keep a very normal, healthy schedule with all of that, I really do. Does that answer your question okay? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the right information.
Is this feeling of being constantly 'on' and unable to slow down something new that started recently, or has it been a pattern you've noticed since childhood or early adulthood?

Well, I suppose... no, it's not exactly new. I mean, I hope it doesn't sound like I'm making a big deal out of nothing, but it's actually been this way for a very long time. 

My mother, bless her heart, she used to joke about it when I was just a little boy in elementary school. She'd say I practically taught the class from my seat because I was just... always up and out of my chair, or talking, or, you know, eagerly jumping in to answer before the teacher even finished giving directions. I was just a very enthusiastic kid, I think. 

But yes, it's definitely been a part of who I am since long before I was an adult. It's not just something that popped up recently. I hope that's helpful? I just want to make sure I'm giving you the full picture, even if it's a little embarrassing to admit I was such a handful as a kid.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on tasks or conversations, or find your mind wandering easily, even when you're trying hard to concentrate?

Well, um... no, not really. I mean, I think I'm actually quite good at staying focused, especially when it comes to my students. You have to be, in special education, you know? You have to really zero in on what they need. 

I suppose sometimes, if a meeting goes on for a very long time, I might get a tiny bit restless, but I think that's normal for anyone, right? I wouldn't say my mind wanders or that I can't concentrate. I'm actually very dedicated to my work and making sure I'm paying attention to the people around me. I really try my best to be present. Is that the kind of thing you were asking about? I just want to be sure I'm answering correctly.
Do you often find yourself interrupting others in conversations, blurting out answers, or having trouble waiting your turn in situations that require patience?

Well, um... I guess I might do that sometimes, but I really only do it because I'm trying to be helpful. I mean, I'm a teacher, so I'm used to stepping in and fixing things, you know? 

Sometimes, if I hear my colleagues talking, or if I'm with parents, or even just at home with my wife and her sister... if I know the answer or I see a solution, I just sort of jump right in. I get a little over-eager, I suppose. I don't mean to be rude, honestly I don't. It's just that I want to help so badly that I end up... well, maybe talking over them a little bit, or taking charge before they've really finished what they were saying. 

I always feel terrible if I realize I've cut someone off. I really do try to be polite and wait my turn. Do you think that's a bad thing? I just want to make sure I'm not coming across as completely overbearing. I really am just trying to be supportive of the people around me.
Have these patterns of restlessness and jumping in ever caused real problems for you—like conflicts with your wife, friction with coworkers, or issues at work—or do people generally not mind it?

Well, um... I really don't want to make it sound like I'm a terrible person to be around, because I really do try my best to be a good husband and a good colleague. But... I suppose it has caused a few, well, some issues. 

At school, they actually... well, they put me on a sort of corrective plan recently. They said the complaints were getting a bit serious. I think my colleagues just feel like I'm taking over too much, even though I'm just trying to be helpful. And at home... my wife, she's wonderful, but she did say that managing the caregiving routines for her sister is just harder because they feel like they have to manage my energy on top of everything else. 

I just feel awful about it. I feel like I'm damaging the trust with the people I care about most—my family, my coworkers—when all I really want to do is help them. Does that make sense? I hope I'm not sounding too difficult. I really do want to fix this and do better.

Inattentive symptoms are denied. Sleep need is normal (ruling out mania/hypomania - no decreased need for sleep, no episodic mood elevation, symptoms are trait-like and chronic rather than episodic). The chronic, non-episodic nature and childhood onset argue against a mood or anxiety disorder diagnosis.
